items.title: Can Jensen Huang Return to Nvidia?
items.summary: The odds of the Nvidia co-founder returning as chief executive appeared to get a boost following new comments by President Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
items.full_text:
Title: Can Jensen Huang Return to Nvidia? - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/business/dealbook/jensen-huang-nvidia.html

Published Time: Mon, 23 Nov 2026 13:31:02 GMT

Markdown Content:
Image

Image

![Image 1: Jensen Huang, in a black leather jacket, standing below the Nvidia logo.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/23/multimedia/23db-huang-kglz/23db-huang-kglz-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

The odds of Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia’s C.E.O. have increased after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appeared to soften his resistance.Credit...Philip Fong/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

**Andrew here.**Is this the week the market hits an inflection point?

Last week’s rout exposed major fault lines: the midterm election’s regulatory threat to data center expansion; tightening export controls on Nvidia’s China sales; and a liquidity drain prompted by Anthropic’s mega-I.P.O. Just as worrying, a strong earnings season has done little to restore investor confidence.

The defining question for Wall Street right now: Are we entering a long-lasting bear market, or is this just a painful, temporary reset? More below.

Image

## The odds of a Huang comeback

Efforts by a vocal group of Silicon Valley moguls (backed by **President Trump**) to get Nvidia to reinstate **Jensen Huang** as C.E.O. appeared to gain steam over the weekend after Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent** seemed to soften his public opposition to the idea.

But new revelations about the Chinese woman involved in the Huang scandal may have muddied the waters again.

**“Jensen is on the outside now,”** Bessent [said on Sunday on the CBS News program “Face the Nation”](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/transcript-treasury-secretary-scott-bessent-face-the-nation-with-margaret-brennan-nov-22-2026/) when asked about his previous demand that Nvidia’s board “[go outside the company](https://www.reuters.com/world/bessent-says-nvidia-must-go-outside-company-find-new-ceo-2026-11-15/)” to find a permanent chief.

Bessent added that Huang’s affair with **Alice Huang**, the chip executive who U.S. intelligence official determined was a spy for China, was essentially a “canard.” The biggest issue, the Treasury secretary said, was determining how Nvidia chips ended up in China despite restrictions on those sales. He suggested that the [buck stopped below the C.E.O.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/business/scott-bessent-jensen-huang-nvidia.html): “What were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?”

*   Bessent’s comments came after repeated support for Huang by Trump, who implored Nvidia’s board on Friday to give the former C.E.O. “[a second chance](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/20/trump-asks-nvidia-to-give-jensen-huang-a-second-chance-01179294),” and wrote on social media on Sunday that it would be “the [best thing for the Company](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117663497310955803), and also, for the U.S.A.”

**Some pro-Huang tech moguls took heart from Bessent’s comments:** “[Progress](https://x.com/travisk/status/2124573240807072074),” **Travis Kalanick**, the Uber co-founder who has publicly demanded the reinstatement of Huang, wrote on social media.

Shares in Nvidia were up 8.6 percent in premarket trading.

**Could a new report change that?**The Times reports, citing people familiar with U.S. intelligence reports, that **Alice Huang** had been in touch with [an official at China’s top spy agency](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/us/politics/alice-huang-china-spy-agency-nvidia.html) for more than a year — at least partly overlapping with her affair with Huang. (**Kang Wei**, a business associate of Alice Huang’s who was often introduced as her husband, also worked with the same agency, the people said.)

**The pressure to reinstate Huang hangs heavily on Nvidia’s board.**An independent review of Huang is underway, even as the company’s new chairman, **Harvey Jones**, declared last week that the board did “[not intend to reinstate Jensen](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/business/nvidia-earnings-jensen-huang.html) as C.E.O.”

Rehiring Huang before the review is complete could add to the board’s legal headaches, if the inquiry finds any wrongdoing. (DealBook hears that what pushed the board to oust Huang was a [report about another affair](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-affair.html) involving a direct report.)

*   Many bettors on prediction markets are increasingly wagering that Huang will return: The implied odds of him becoming Nvidia’s next C.E.O. have hit 17 percent on [Kalshi](https://kalshi.com/markets/kxnvdaceo/next-nvidia-ceo/kxnvdaceo-29jan) and 19 percent on [Polymarket](https://polymarket.com/event/next-ceo-of-nvidia), putting him in the lead. (The previous front-runner, Rene Haas, just agreed to [stay on at the chip designer Arm](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261123611198/en/Arm-CEO-Rene-Haas-Affirms-Long-Term-Commitment-to-Lead-Companys-Next-Phase-of-Growth) through 2033.)

**The stakes of the Nvidia leadership question are huge.**The chip maker’s processors power a majority of the artificial intelligence world’s leading applications, while its balance sheet is single-handedly propping up a huge portion of A.I. start-ups. (Though Wall Street is increasingly divided over the wisdom of the trillion-dollar chip financing boom — more on that below.)

Image

### HERE’S WHAT’S HAPPENING

**Climate talks collapse.** COP31, this year’s United Nations climate summit, broke down [without a final agreement](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/climate/cop31-climate-summit-ends-climate.html). The European Union and small countries vulnerable to climate disasters rejected a proposal that blocked any mention of fossil fuels, a root cause of global warming. The impasse underscores the tension in efforts to transition to more renewable energy sources as **President Trump** and oil-producing giants such as Saudi Arabia promote fossil fuels.

**An Anthropic researcher claims to have deciphered a major mathematics problem.**A mathematician at Anthropic, **Levent Alpoge**, said he had used Claude to [solve the super-complicated Riemann hypothesis](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/science/anthropic-ai-math-riemann-hypothesis.html). If the claim is verified, it will be the latest remarkable advance by artificial intelligence in the field of mathematics this year. Speaking of numbers, Wall Street expects that the bonds Anthropic sells to [fund its $900 billion spending commitments](https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/anthropic-committed-to-spend-900-billion-wall-street-expects-its-debt-to-be-junk-5514d55d?mod=hp_lead_pos2) to be rated at junk.

**Trump finds an issue where he can work with Democrats.**Trump said he would collaborate with Democrats to [cap interest and fees on credit cards](https://www.axios.com/2026/11/21/trump-credit-cards-rates-warren), an issue long pushed by Senator **Elizabeth Warren**, the Massachusetts Democrat set to be the new chair of the Banking Committee. (The banking industry claimed that such a move would deny credit to millions of people with poor credit ratings.) The bipartisan gesture came as the Democrats [won their 258th seat](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/us/politics/democrats-midterm-house-majority-record.html) in the House with the election of **Chuck Hubbard** in North Carolina, clinching their largest majority since 1992.

**CrowdStrike acquires a rival.**The cybersecurity firm agreed to buy Zscaler for [about $44 billion](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/business/crowdstrike-zscaler-cybersecurity.html) in stock. Shares in CrowdStrike fell more than 6 percent in premarket trading on the news. Analysts are wondering if the tie-up presages a string of deals in the sector, as advanced A.I. models make it increasingly easy for hackers to break into corporate and government systems.

Image

## Wall Street giants are split over A.I. chip deals

The Nasdaq Composite [looks set to rebound](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/business/ai-stocks-sp500.html) on Monday. But Wall Street is [still fretting](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/business/anthropic-ai-stocks-sp500.html) about the artificial intelligence trade after [Anthropic’s record-breaking I.P.O.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/anthropic-ipo-pricing.html?) fizzled amid a huge sell-off last week in tech stocks.

Investors are worried about the economics of the A.I. buildout, including the financing and [life span of A.I. chips](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/11/14/ai-gpu-depreciation-coreweave-nvidia-michael-burry.html) — the brunt of which come from Nvidia — that power the technology. Against that backdrop, two Wall Street heavyweights, Apollo Global Management and Ares Management, have staked out drastically different positions, Niko Gallogly reports.

Trillions of dollars are expected to flow into A.I. over the next several years. For every dollar spent, [about 60 cents](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/technology-media-and-telecommunications/our-insights/the-cost-of-compute-a-7-trillion-dollar-race-to-scale-data-centers) will go toward chips, according to McKinsey.

**But Ares Management sees major risks in those investments.** The firm [recently argued](https://www.ares.com/content/dam/aresmgmt/Documents/In-the-Gaps/Ares_InTheGaps_Newsletter_Fall-2026.pdf) in its In the Gaps newsletter that chips were “one the fastest-depreciating assets we can name” and that “financing markets have the shortest track record and least experience,” underwriting them.

“I, for one, personally do not know how to underwrite the decline in depreciation curves on that type of technology,” **Michael Arougheti**, the C.E.O. of Ares, told analysts last month.

Apollo’s C.E.O., **Marc Rowan**, called out the Ares newsletter in the firm’s earnings call this month: “Not to make fun of t

items.title: Two Major Cybersecurity Firms to Combine in $44 Billion Deal
items.summary: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler, bulking up as worries about hacks fueled by advances in artificial intelligence bedevil companies and governments.
items.full_text:
Title: Two Major Cybersecurity Firms to Combine in $44 Billion Deal - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/business/crowdstrike-zscaler-cybersecurity.html

Published Time: Mon, 23 Nov 2026 13:28:22 GMT

Markdown Content:
CrowdStrike agreed on Monday to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at $43.9 billion, uniting two major cybersecurity providers as worries about hacks perpetuated by artificial intelligence weigh heavily in corporate boardrooms and government offices around the world.

Rapid advances in A.I. models from OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as from their Chinese rivals, have stoked concern about the state of global defenses against cyberattacks.

In recent weeks, a series of [outages](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/us/politics/tech-outages-trump-national-security.html) hit [banking transactions](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/bank-outages-down.html), [Microsoft](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/microsoft-outage-what-to-know.html) products, [Apple](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/microsoft-outage-what-to-know.html) services, a key system at the [National Security Agency](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/us/politics/nsa-down-network-outage-nsanet.html?) and [commercial air traffic](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/faa-ground-stop-flights-what-to-know.html) in the United States. For the most part, these disruptions appeared to result from software patches going awry as institutions tried to harden their systems against new vulnerabilities, rather than malicious cyberattacks.

But the urgency of preparing for potential waves of attacks has led company leaders and government officials to spend more on cybersecurity, prompting companies in the field to combine to offer customers one-stop shops for protecting their systems. Over the past two years, Google agreed to pay [$32 billion](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/18/technology/google-alphabet-wiz-deal.html) to buy Wiz, while Palo Alto Networks struck a [$25 billion takeover of CyberArk](https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/company/press/2025/palo-alto-networks-announces-agreement-to-acquire-cyberark--the-identity-security-leader).

By acquiring Zscaler, CrowdStrike, which focuses on protecting personal computers and servers, is seeking to add cloud-based protection for corporate networks. It would rank among the largest deals ever in the cybersecurity industry.

“We see a path to become the largest A.I. safety and security company the world has ever seen,” George Kurtz, the founder and chief executive of CrowdStrike, said in a statement.

Under the [terms of the agreement](https://ir.crowdstrike.com/news-releases/news-release-details/crowdstrike-acquire-zscaler-bringing-network-security-and-zero), CrowdStrike will issue 1.135 new shares for each share of Zscaler. That represents a premium of roughly 34 percent to Zscaler’s closing price on Friday, before the deal was announced.

Shares in Zscaler jumped more than 16 percent in premarket trading on Monday, but CrowdStrike’s stock fell nearly 7 percent on the news.

The deal is expected to close by January 2028, pending regulatory approvals.

The transaction, one of the biggest acquisitions of the year, also underscores the appetite in corporate America for consolidation to bolster growth. Deal makers on Wall Street have said that they expect merger discussions to increase as companies race to wrap up deals before the end of the Trump administration, which has been seen as friendly to large-scale mergers and acquisitions.

items.title: In Vietnam, an Electric Vehicle Revolution Without Cars
items.summary: An oil shock is speeding a transformation of Vietnam’s streets, challenging global motorcycle giants and lifting a new generation of domestic manufacturers.
items.full_text:
Title: In Vietnam, an Electric Vehicle Revolution Without Cars - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/business/electric-motorcyles-vietnam.html

Published Time: Mon, 23 Nov 2026 13:10:01 GMT

Markdown Content:
In Vietnam, life moves on two wheels. Tens of millions of motorbikes swarm the streets, carrying commuters to the office, children to school and delivery riders from one order to the next.

For generations, they have run on gasoline. Now, more and more are plugging in instead of filling up.

Soaring oil prices, a government drive to curb pollution and a new generation of hometown manufacturers are accelerating the shift. This year, one in three new two-wheelers sold in Vietnam is electric, turning one of the world’s largest motorcycle markets into a testing ground for the future of transportation.

The transformation is challenging an industry dominated by Japanese manufacturers like Honda and Yamaha, while creating an opening for Vietnamese companies like VinFast and Dat Bike.

And it has gained new momentum from a war thousands of miles away.

Video

[Video 11](https://vp.nyt.com/video/hlsfmp4/2026/11/20/180846_1_23vid-vietnam-ebike_wg_av1-1080p/master.m3u8)

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/16/multimedia/Biz-Vietnam-EV-05-vlqb/Biz-Vietnam-EV-05-vlqb-verticalTwoByThree735.jpg?auto=webp&quality=30&disable=upscale&format=pjpg)How Homeowners Are Powering Vietnam’s E-Bike Surge

1:22

The war in Iran has brought on a rapid switch from motorbikes to electric two-wheelers in Vietnam, creating an informal charging economy led by entrepreneurial homeowners.Credit Credit...Chang W. Lee/The New York Times

The United States’ war with Iran has disrupted oil supplies and sent the price of gasoline soaring, making electric motorcycles an [increasingly attractive alternative](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/11/climate/electric-motorcycles-pakistan.html). At the same time, authorities in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam’s two biggest cities, are pushing to phase out gas-powered vehicles. Enforcement remains a challenge, but the policies are nudging consumers toward electric alternatives and spurring investment in infrastructure needed to support them.

If government policy laid the groundwork, rising gasoline prices have given the transition a powerful jolt.

More than 973,000 e-motorbikes were sold in the first nine months of this year, a 91 percent increase over the same period last year, according to MotorCycles Data.

Around the world, surging prices at the pump have driven interest in electric vehicles. From Sydney to London to Rio de Janeiro, growing numbers of drivers are turning to electric cars, many from Chinese manufacturers.

In Vietnam, though, electrification is unfolding on two wheels. And local companies, not Chinese giants like BYD and Geely, are some of the biggest beneficiaries.

![Image 2: An employee inserting a tall, square gray battery into a white electric scooter.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/16/multimedia/Biz-Vietnam-EV-02-vlqb/Biz-Vietnam-EV-02-vlqb-mobileMasterAt3x.jpg?auto=avif&quality=75)[Video 12](https://vp.nyt.com/video/2026/11/19/183938_1_18visualUploader-37723_wg_1080p.mp4)

VinFast said it plans to sell 1.5 million electric motorbikes in 2026.

For Phung Quang Duyen, 54, the appeal was immediate. On a recent Sunday in Hanoi, a makeshift stand displaying Dat Bike’s latest model caught his eye. He circled the red motorbike, took some videos on his phone and climbed aboard for a test ride. Its acceleration was so powerful that Mr. Phung had lurched backward during the ride.

When he returned, he excitedly called his wife.

Their daughter was about to start her first job, and the couple had planned to buy her a Honda Vision, one of Vietnam’s most popular gas-powered motorcycles. But the Dat Bike cost about $1,160, roughly the same as the Honda.

And unlike the Honda, it would never need gasoline.

“Now I need to check and convince my wife,” Mr. Duyen said with a laugh, hurrying off with a packet of brochures.

For other riders, switching to electric is becoming an economic necessity.

![Image 3](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/16/multimedia/Biz-Vietnam-EV-04-vlqb/Biz-Vietnam-EV-04-vlqb-mobileMasterAt3x.jpg?auto=avif&quality=75)[Video 13](https://vp.nyt.com/video/2026/11/16/183707_1_16visualUploader-18714_wg_1080p.mp4)

Phung Quang Duyen tested a Dat Bike for his daughter on a recent Sunday morning in Hanoi. 

Image

![Image 4: Rows of black motorbikes, their seats covered in plastic, are parked inside an industrial building.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/16/multimedia/Biz-Vietnam-EV-phvf/Biz-Vietnam-EV-phvf-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Electric motorbikes at a Dat Bike factory in Ho Chi Minh City.

Nguyen Van Sy,26, rides a run-down brown Honda handed down by his parents. He relies on it to commute to his job as a chef at a catering company and to make deliveries for Grab on the side.

But keeping it fueled is eating into his earnings.

“The increase in petroleum has affected my work,” Mr. Sy said during a stop at a Hanoi gas station. Before the war in Iran, filling his tank cost about $3.90. Now it can cost as much as $5.41 — a steep increase for someone who depends on his motorcycle to earn a living.

“I am planning to buy an e-bike now,” he said. First, he needs to save enough to afford one.

For electric motorbike manufacturers, that financial pressure has translated into a rush of customers.

Dat Bike’s sales surged when gas prices rose 40 percent in March, said Nguyen Son, the company’s founder.

“We didn’t even have the inventory to sell,” he said. “It’s very clear that, eventually, we have to move to electric vehicles.”

But Vietnam’s electric motorcycle boom is about more than a temporary spike in gas prices.

Image

Testing the motorbike batteries.

Image

Assembling an electric motorbike.

Image

“The increase in petroleum has affected my work,” said Nguyen Van Sy, who is saving up to buy an electric bike.

Once dismissed as little more than souped-up versions of the electric bicycles and scooters favored by high school students, electric motorcycles can rival gasoline-powered models in power and performance. Many can be charged at home, while others have removable batteries that riders can swap for fully charged ones in minutes.

The expanding range of models is beginning to challenge the dominance of established manufacturers like Honda.

“In Vietnam, we’ve had more than 50 years of Honda bikes, so the change to VinFast or other electric vehicles is hard,” said Hoang Ha, deputy chief executive of VinFast E-Motorcycle Vietnam.

To ease that transition, manufacturers are pouring money into charging networks and offering sweeteners, seeking to overcome the fear of running out of power, a major barrier to electric vehicle adoption.

VinFast offers a battery-swapping program that includes 20 free swaps a month, enough to cover many riders’ daily commutes. The company says it has already rolled out 60,000 bright blue battery-swapping stations this year and aims to reach 150,000 by year’s end.

[Video 14](https://vp.nyt.com/video/2026/11/19/183939_1_18visualUploader-43736_wg_1080p.mp4)![Image 5: Several people taking batteries out of a row of tall devices that look like vending machines. It is nighttime, and the green glow from the devices is reflected on the people's clothing.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/16/multimedia/Biz-Vietnam-EV-07-vlqb/Biz-Vietnam-EV-07-vlqb-mobileMasterAt3x.jpg?auto=avif&quality=75)

There are tens of thousands of battery swapping stations across Vietnam. Some bikes have batteries that can be removed for charging at battery swapping stations.

“At first you have to push people, and it takes time and costs a lot,” Mr. Ha said. He added that VinFast was willing to shoulder that expense to attract customers and encourage greener transportation.

Beyond corporate charging networks, a more informal charging economy is springing up.

In Ho Chi Minh City, some cafes let customers charge their motorcycles while they have a coffee. Enterprising families have begun selling access to their electricity, with some offering food, showers and even beds to waiting riders.

On a recent Wednesday evening, there were 20 lined up inside the home of Le Huy Hoi on the outskirts of the city, plugged into outlets along his living room wall.

He started his business two years ago, catering to students, nearby apartment residents and app-based drivers. Demand grew so quickly that he repeatedly moved to larger premises. His current home is the third location.

He, his wife and their two sons share two rooms. A third bedroom has been converted into a dormitory with 15 bunk beds. He also offers food and showers.

The business earns about $400 a month in profit. But even after expanding twice, Mr. Hoi said, he can’t keep up.

An e-bike charging store provides, food, shower and beds, while Motorbikes are the main mode of transport for Vietnamese families.

“As you can see, I am not able to provide the market demand,” he said, pointing to a line of bikes outside his front door. As he spoke, several more drivers walked into his living room, looking for a place to plug in.
